title: EdDSA and Ed25519
one_liner: Schnorr-style signatures on Edwards curves with deterministic nonces, computed at full size against RFC 8032, and the API mistake that leaked keys anyway.
description: EdDSA and Ed25519: Schnorr signatures on a twisted Edwards curve, deterministic nonce derivation, RFC 8032's test vectors reproduced at full size, and private-key recovery from signing APIs that accept the public key as a separate argument.
standfirst: Ed25519 was designed after a decade of ECDSA keys lost to bad random numbers. Its nonce is derived from the key and the message, so a signer with a broken random number generator is still safe. The best-known flaw since then has been in how libraries let it be called.

facts.Rests on: The ECDLP on Curve25519 (or Curve448 for Ed448)
facts.Best known attack: Pollard's rho, about 2<sup>126</sup> for Ed25519. In practice, fault attacks and API misuse

blocks.p: EdDSA is a Schnorr signature. A key is a 32-byte secret, hashed with SHA-512 into two halves: a scalar a, clamped as in X25519, and a 32-byte prefix. The public key A = aG is the encoded curve point. To sign a message M:

steps: Derive the nonce deterministically: r = SHA-512(prefix ‖ M) mod L.
Compute the challenge k = SHA-512(R ‖ A ‖ M) mod L.
Compute S = r + k·a mod L. The signature is R ‖ S, 64 bytes.

blocks.p: The verifier checks that SG = R + kA. Compared with ECDSA there is no modular inversion, the signature is a point and a scalar rather than two scalars, and the challenge hashes the public key, which binds each signature to one key.

The code that builds this page implements RFC 8032 directly, in twisted Edwards coordinates on the same field as X25519. It reproduces the first {{vectors}} Ed25519 test vectors of the RFC byte for byte. Here is test 1, the signature on the empty message:

blocks.label: RFC 8032 section 7.1, test 1, recomputed at build time

blocks.p: The nonce is the part of ECDSA that fails in practice: a repeated or biased k gives up the key. EdDSA derives r from the secret prefix and the message, so it cannot repeat across different messages without a SHA-512 collision, and it needs no random number generator at all. Signing "{{msg}}" twice with the key of RFC test 2 produces the same 64 bytes both times, and the build checks it.

The cost is the one discussed on the ECDSA page: identical computations invite fault attacks, since a single glitched signature can be compared with a correct one on the same message. Hedged variants add randomness to the derivation for devices exposed to faults.

Determinism has a precondition that the API has to enforce: the public key hashed into the challenge must be the signer's own. In 2022 researchers at Mysten Labs reported that dozens of Ed25519 libraries exposed signing functions taking the secret key and the public key as separate arguments, and did not check that they matched. Their list reached 45 affected libraries by 2023, and the issue was later presented to NIST by Chalkias, Garillot and Nikolaenko.

If an attacker can get the same message signed twice, once with the right public key A and once with any other A′, the nonce r is the same, because it depends only on the prefix and the message. The challenge differs, because it hashes the public key. The two signatures share R and give two equations:

blocks.math: S<sub>1</sub> = r + k<sub>1</sub>a,   S<sub>2</sub> = r + k<sub>2</sub>a  ⇒  a = (S<sub>1</sub> − S<sub>2</sub>) / (k<sub>1</sub> − k<sub>2</sub>) mod L
blocks.label: The same algebra as ECDSA nonce reuse

blocks.p: The build does exactly this with the key of RFC test 2, signing "{{msg}}" once with its own public key and once with the public key of test 3:

blocks.label: Two signatures on one message with different public keys, and the scalar recovered from them (little-endian encodings for R and S)

blocks.p: The recovered a satisfies aG = A. It is the signing scalar, and it is all a forger needs, since any nonce works: the build signs "{{forged_msg}}" with it, and the signature verifies under the victim's public key. The fix is to derive the public key from the secret inside the signing function, or to check that the two match.

EdDSA's verification has more edge cases than its signing, because of the cofactor 8 and non-canonical encodings. Implementations have disagreed on whether to check SG = R + kA or 8SG = 8R + 8kA, whether to accept S ≥ L, and which encodings of R and A to accept. For most uses this does not matter. For consensus systems, where every node must reach the same verdict on every signature, it does. RFC 8032 requires rejecting S ≥ L, which prevents the malleability that affects ECDSA, and later work has pinned down the remaining rules.

Ed25519 is the default signature in SSH keys, in Signal, in Tor and in many blockchains, and it has been in FIPS 186-5 since 2023. Its classical security is that of the ECDLP on Curve25519, about 2126. Like every elliptic-curve scheme it falls to Shor's algorithm, and NIST IR 8547 proposes disallowing it after 2035 in favour of ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.
